entries.t: One in Five: IEPs and 504 Plans in America
entries.x: The federal government's newest civil-rights count says 19% of American public-school students — nearly one in five — now have a disability plan: an IEP under IDEA or a plan under Section 504. That share was 17% just one collection earlier. The question…
entries.w: one in five: ieps and 504 plans in america one in five : ieps and 504 plans in america the federal government's newest civil-rights count says 19% of american public-school students — nearly one in five — now have a disability plan: an iep under idea or a plan under section 504. that share was 17% just one collection earlier. the question dividing researchers is why. is the country finally counting real need it used to miss — or is a strained school system manufacturing disability out of weak instruction, loose eligibility, and incentives? the evidence, weighed below, points to a mixed answer with a clear tilt. source for all four figures: u.s. department of education, office for civil rights, a first look: the civil rights data collection, 2023–24 (49.7 million students; 17,591 districts; 97,094 schools). the 19% total is up from 17% in the prior (2021–22) collection, per disability scoop, oct. 19, 2026 . the recent rise is driven mainly by expanded identification of real need — autism, adhd, developmental delay, and section 504 plans. but who gets identified, where , and under which label is shaped powerfully by the system itself: state rules, local practice, family resources, and classroom context. the strongest single piece of evidence is the category pattern. specific learning disability — the one category the “poor instruction” theory predicts should be swelling — has been shrinking for two decades , down roughly 450,000 students between 2002 and 2023 even as total idea enrollment grew by about 1.1 million. growth is concentrated where diagnostic criteria broadened, screening improved, and the law widened: autism (up more than eightfold in count), other health impairment (the adhd category, more than tripled), and 504-only plans (nearly quadrupled since 2009–10). one in five one in five

entries.w: restraint & seclusion in america's school districts restraint & seclusion in america's school districts a public comparison of reported restraint and seclusion rates — not just counts — for school districts in the 2023–24 civil rights data collection, with each district's reporting status shown. all figures are as districts reported them to the u.s. department of education. the go to place for any issue having to do with education across the nation a public comparison of reported restraint and seclusion rates — not just counts — for school districts in the 2023–24 civil rights data collection, with each district's reporting status shown. rates are students reported per 1,000 enrolled students. this page also shows each district's idea disparity ratio and its change from 2020–21, and it shows reported zeros and districts with no valid report as what they are — reports, not findings. this figure sums the student counts for physical restraint, mechanical restraint, and seclusion. a student reported in more than one practice type is counted once in each type, so this is not a count of unique students. rates and the idea disparity ratio built on this figure use the same summed basis. restraint and seclusion restraint and seclusion

entries.t: Press Kit
entries.x: Press kit for Education Across the States: show facts, flagship investigations, sourcing standard, and producer contact.
entries.w: press kit education across the states press kit for education across the states: show facts, flagship investigations, sourcing standard, and producer contact. the go to place for any issue having to do with education across the nation built from the federal civil rights data collection (2023–24) and idea section 618 child counts: 19% of public school students have an iep or a section 504 plan — 15% under idea (about 7.6 million students) and 4% section 504-only (about 1.9 million). the investigation tests the two explanations against the category data: specific learning disability has fallen by roughly 450,000 students since 2002 while autism rose more than eightfold; state identification rates run from about 11% to about 21% under one federal law; texas's decade-long 8.5% benchmark suppressed identification until federal monitors intervened, after which texas grew 67% in eight years. students with ieps account for 73% of physical restraints in the federal data. full charts, expert voices, and sources: educationacrossthestates.com/one-in-five/ section 504-only identification almost quadrupled in fifteen years — 1.1% of students in 2009–10 to about 4% today — under a legal test that has not changed. rates run from 0% to over 30% by school building, skew affluent and white against the iep pattern, and the system has no federal funding trail, no published national condition breakdown, and has never had an eligibility audit. every on-air claim proof-checked against its source before publication. sources in every episode. each episode description names its documents, datasets, and reporting. nothing invented — no fabricated quotes or figures. real voices, unaltered — guest recordings air exactly as submitted; written answers are read verbatim. right of reply — institutions and officials we cover are invited on the record, and responses air as given. corrections in the open. press kit.html press kit.html

entries.t: Privacy & How We Protect Your Information
entries.x: What personal information the Education Across the States forms collect, why we collect it, and how we protect it.
entries.w: privacy & how we protect your information privacy & how we protect your information what personal information the education across the states forms collect, why we collect it, and how we protect it. the go to place for any issue having to do with education across the nation education across the states is produced by professional development inc. producer: charles mayfield. this page explains what personal information our forms collect, why, and how we protect it. through our internship application form: your name and email, school and program, a résumé and optional writing sample, a copy of your state-issued id (driver's license or state id card). a state-issued id shows your full legal name, photograph, date of birth, home address, id number, and physical description; uploading a copy gives us all of that information. we use the copy only to verify age and identity (see id copies, below). through our call-request form: your name, email, phone number, organization and role (optional), what you'd like to discuss, your best times and time zone, and any extra notes you choose to add. google forms requires you to sign in to a google account to upload files, and google records the name, email address, and profile photo of the account you use together with your submission. privacy.html privacy.html

entries.t: The Records Project
entries.x: The Education Records Project: the same public-records request to every state and territorial education agency in the United States, and everything produced, published free. Education Across the States — the go to place for any issue having to do with…
entries.w: the records project the records project the education records project: the same public-records request to every state and territorial education agency in the united states, and everything produced, published free. education across the states — the go to place for any issue having to do with education across the nation. the go to place for any issue having to do with education across the nation we asked every state education agency in the country — plus the district of columbia and the five u.s. territories — for the same core records. everything they produce is published here, in full, free: the spending ledgers, the grant files, the monitoring reports, the complaint decisions. this is the collection, and it is open to anyone who wants to check the work — ours included. the same ten items, of every agency, in electronic form where it exists: the check register and purchase orders; agency credit-card records; the payroll listing; adopted budgets and budget-versus-actual reports; federal grant files — idea part b allocations to districts, osep monitoring reports with the state's responses and corrective action plans, and determination letters; state complaint and due-process hearing decisions, as the agency keeps them; copies of any and all vendor contracts signed, regardless of dollar value; state board minutes; and the agency's organizational chart. same questions everywhere, so the answers can be compared. the full index is the document register in the education records repository — every document, the request that produced it, and the date it arrived. every document carries a register id (for example, erp-nh-0001). records project.html records project.html

entries.t: McKinney-Vento: What the Law Requires
entries.x: A briefing on the McKinney-Vento Act's education subtitle: who qualifies, the core rights every district owes, the misunderstandings that produce findings and lawsuits, and what full compliance looks like in board policy and daily practice.
entries.w: mckinney-vento: what the law requires mckinney-vento: the students the law already covers a briefing on the mckinney-vento act's education subtitle: who qualifies, the core rights every district owes, the misunderstandings that produce findings and lawsuits, and what full compliance looks like in board policy and daily practice. what the law requires, where districts get it wrong, and what full compliance looks like in policy and practice the mckinney-vento homeless assistance act's education subtitle — the education for homeless children and youths program, 42 u.s.c. §§ 11431–11435, as amended by the every student succeeds act — is a barrier-removal and school-stability law. it is not a housing program, and it is not a program only for districts that win a federal subgrant. its core duties — identify, enroll immediately, keep the student in the school of origin when that is in the student's best interest, transport on request, provide comparable services, and resolve disputes enroll-first — bind every local education agency in a state receiving program funds, whether or not the agency receives a subgrant . it is also one of the most widely misunderstood laws in american education. most students it covers are not in shelters. most compliance failures are not exotic: they are a front desk asking for a lease, a transportation office waiting on another district, a policy manual that has not been opened since before the 2016 amendments. this briefing states what the law says, documents the failures with the audit and court record, and then sets out the compliance build — the board policy, identification system, and daily procedures that keep a district on the right side of all three. national figures are the most recent available: school year 2023–24, from edfacts data reported by state and local agencies and summarized by the national center for homeless education (march 2026), analyzed by schoolhouse connection. no national summary for 2024–25 has been released. by every account in the sources, the 2023–24 count is still an undercount. mckinney vento.html mckinney vento.html

entries.t: Maryland's Board Meets Thursday: Report Card, Phones, and a Literacy Vote
entries.x: On October 29, the Maryland State Board of Education reviews the 2026 Maryland Report Card, considers adopting a combined PreK-12 literacy policy, and reviews phone-free schools regulations.
entries.w: maryland's board meets thursday: report card, phones, and a literacy vote maryland's board meets thursday: report card, phones, and a literacy vote on october 29, the maryland state board of education reviews the 2026 maryland report card, considers adopting a combined prek-12 literacy policy, and reviews phone-free schools regulations. the most consequential maryland education meeting of the month has not happened yet. on monday, october 26, the maryland state department of education announced that the maryland state board of education will meet thursday, october 29, at 9 a.m. at the nancy s. grasmick state education building, 200 west baltimore street in baltimore, in the board room on the seventh floor, with a complete agenda and a livestream available online. three items on that agenda will reach into almost every classroom in the state. first, the board will review the 2026 maryland report card, the state's public rating for every school, expressed as one to five stars. the stars are not a single test score: elementary and middle schools combine academic achievement, academic progress, progress in achieving english language proficiency, and school quality and student success, while high schools add graduation rate and readiness for postsecondary success. the board will also review maryland comprehensive assessment program results for high school science and american government — subjects tied to graduation requirements. the announcement did not include the new results themselves, so thursday is when the state puts its own reading of them on the record. second, the board will consider adopting the comprehensive prek through 12 literacy policy. the early-grades piece, covering prekindergarten through third grade, was adopted on october 22, 2024. a draft adolescent literacy policy was combined with it in april 2026, following public comment and stakeholder input, with further versions in june and in july and august. if the board adopts the combined policy on thursday, districts will work from a single statewide literacy policy from prekindergarten through twelfth grade. third, the board will review regulations to implement the maryland phone-free schools act, passed this year and effective july 1, 2026. the law requires each local board to develop, by the 2027–28 school year, a policy prohibiting students from using electronic communication devices from the first bell to the last, including instructional periods, lunch, recess, and passing periods, with protected exceptions for a purpose documented in a student's individualized education program, for a health need covered by a section 504 plan, or in an emergency. the board will also receive an update on teacher recruitment and vacancies, following the department's october 19 announcement that statewide vacancies had fallen from 2,145 in 2022–23 to 572 this year. news 2026 10 27 maryland board meeting.html news 2026 10 27 maryland board meeting.html

entries.t: [New Hampshire] Deep Dive — State Complaints, ESY, and Compensatory Education
entries.x: This deep dive walks through the three dispute tools that meet in one file folder: the state complaint under 34 CFR 300.151 through 300.153 and New Hampshire's Ed 1121 process (who can file, the sixty-day clock, the commissioner's signed decision, the…
entries.w: [new hampshire] deep dive — state complaints, esy, and compensatory education this deep dive walks through the three dispute tools that meet in one file folder: the state complaint under 34 cfr 300.151 through 300.153 and new hampshire's ed 1121 process (who can file, the sixty-day clock, the commissioner's signed decision, the twenty-day reconsideration rule, and the public complaint summaries required by rsa 186-c:5-a); extended school year under 34 cfr 300.106 and new hampshire's ed 1110.01 (individual team determination, the regression and recoupment standard, and the factors beyond regression); and compensatory education under the qualitative "but for" standard of reid v. district of columbia, 401 f.3d 516 (d.c. cir. 2005), including the first circuit's pihl decision and real new hampshire complaint orders that required districts to deliver compensatory services. the episode closes with the documentation habits that decide these cases in practice. plain-english explanations of the governing rules, with settled law distinguished from practical interpretation, for working new hampshire special education teachers and case managers. ### sources - 34 cfr 300.151–300.153 (state complaint procedures, remedies, and filing contents): https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/34/300.152 — also search ecfr at ecfr.gov for "300.151 adoption of state complaint procedures" and "300.153 complaint contents" to read the adopted text of all three sections side by side. - new hampshire rules for the education of children with disabilities, ed 1121 (complaint process) and ed 1110.01 (extended school year): full rule text at https://www.gc.nh.gov/rules/state_agencies/ed1100.html — find ed 1121 in part ed 1121 and ed 1110.01 in part ed 1110 on that page; entries.t: The Plan Nobody Audits: Section 504's Quiet Quadrupling
entries.x: This deep dive examines the fastest-growing accommodation system in American public schools: plans under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 held by students who do not have IEPs. Drawing on the U.S. Department of Education's Civil Rights Data…
entries.w: the plan nobody audits: section 504's quiet quadrupling this deep dive examines the fastest-growing accommodation system in american public schools: plans under section 504 of the rehabilitation act of 1973 held by students who do not have ieps. drawing on the u.s. department of education's civil rights data collection for 2023–24 and the leading published research, alex and jordan walk through what a section 504 plan is and how its three-part eligibility test differs from the idea; how the "504-only" rate climbed from 1.1% of students in 2009–10 to 3.9% in 2021–22 and about 1.9 million students (4%) in 2023–24; why rates range from near double the national average in texas and new hampshire to below half in new mexico and mississippi, with individual texas middle schools above 30% and other schools at zero; the documented skew toward white students (60% of 504-only students against 44% of enrollment) and, in the first study to link school records to irs tax data, toward higher-income families (2.9% vs. 1.5%), even as ieps run the opposite way; the measured response of 504 enrollment to the college board's 2017 decision to honor school accommodations on the sat automatically; the costs of both over-identification and under-identification; and the central evidentiary gap — no national breakdown of 504 plans by condition and no national audit of 504 eligibility has ever been published, so claims about how many plans are "unnecessary" exceed what the evidence can support. plain-english explanations, with every number sourced and the limits of the evidence stated on air. ### sources - u.s. department of education, office for civil rights, "a first look: the civil rights data collection, 2023–24" (september 2026) — 19% of students with disabilities (15% idea; 4% / ~1.9m section 504 only); white students 60% of 504-only vs. 44% of enrollment; boys 56% of 504-only: https://www.ed.gov/media/document/2023-24-first-look-civil-rights-data-collection-september-30-2026-114593.pdf - perry a. zirkel, "concerns about misidentification of '504-only' students," atpe news, march 30, 2026 — 1.1% (2009–10) to 3.9% (2021–22); texas 7.6%; 23 of the top 25 districts (14.4%–17.4%); texas middle schools at 23.1%–30.1%; three-part eligibility test; no federal/state funding; costs of over- and under-identification; texas dyslexia analysis: https://atpenews.org/concerns-about-misidentif

entries.t: The List Nobody Can See: Inside the Child Care Food Program's Seven-Year Blacklist
entries.x: One routine Federal Register notice this fall renewed the paperwork behind the National Disqualified List — the Child and Adult Care Food Program's national bar on institutions, sponsoring organizations, day care home providers, and the individuals who run…
entries.w: the list nobody can see: inside the child care food program's seven-year blacklist one routine federal register notice this fall renewed the paperwork behind the national disqualified list — the child and adult care food program's national bar on institutions, sponsoring organizations, day care home providers, and the individuals who run them. this deep dive opens up the machine: how a review finding becomes a "serious deficiency," how the corrective-action clock runs, why quitting does not save you, the appeal you get — and the six decisions 7 cfr 226.6(k)(3) says you can never appeal — and how a listing lasts seven years, or longer if a program debt is unpaid. plus the vagueness problem the national cacfp association put in writing (the same citation can mean a serious management problem in one state or "three small errors on a reimbursement claims form" in another), the patchwork early-removal door, the feeding our future record that explains why the list exists, and the 2024 proposed rule (fns-2024-0005) that would rebuild the process — still unfinalized. usda does not publish the list or its size; where the public record runs out, this episode says so. sources: - 7 cfr 226.6 (cacfp state agency responsibilities — serious deficiency process at (c), national disqualified list at (c)(7), administrative review at (k), day care home reviews at (l)): https://www.casemine.com/regulation/us/640f05fa8b0a3c5be33657ac/amp (also available at ecfr, title 7, part 226, §226.6) - usda food and nutrition service, "proposed rule: serious deficiency process in the cacfp and sfsp" (docket fns-2024-0005; entries.t: [Rhode Island] Education Daily — October 23, 2026: The Squeeze Before the Formula Changes

entries.w: [rhode island] education daily — october 23, 2026: the squeeze before the formula changes rhode island districts are cutting staff and hunting for savings as energy, transportation, health care, and special education costs climb for fiscal 2027 — cranston cut six point four million dollars including thirty paraprofessionals, warwick reports special education costs up fourteen percent since fiscal 2024, and the funding formula review that might change the math will not report for nearly a year — plus providence opens applications for two school board seats that begin in january. sources: - entries.t: [Tennessee] Education Daily — October 23, 2026: The Firm Behind the Takeover, a Retention Rebound That Isn't Finished, and a Shrinking Cohort
entries.x: Three Tennessee stories about capacity: Chalkbeat Tennessee reports that MGT, the Florida consulting firm that helped launch Houston's state takeover, has been drafting bylaws, contract rules, and an executive director job description for the Memphis-Shelby…
entries.w: [tennessee] education daily — october 23, 2026: the firm behind the takeover, a retention rebound that isn't finished, and a shrinking cohort three tennessee stories about capacity: chalkbeat tennessee reports that mgt, the florida consulting firm that helped launch houston's state takeover, has been drafting bylaws, contract rules, and an executive director job description for the memphis-shelby county oversight board since july — work the board accepted eight to one, funded by local philanthropy rather than the board itself; a nashville focal analysis of state data finds teacher retention has risen from its 2023-24 low but has not returned to earlier levels; and a tennessee firefly report on excelined data shows a shrinking young cohort — 83,021 births in 2023, kindergarten enrollment down five percent — pressing districts from memphis, which closed five schools last year, to the growth counties of middle tennessee, nine days before every district's funding-formula accountability report is due to the state on november 1. sources: - chalkbeat tennessee (october 23, 2026) — reporting on mgt's work for the state-appointed memphis-shelby county schools oversight board: bylaws, the $50,000 contract-approval process, the executive director job description, the 8-1 board vote, philanthropic funding via seeding success, and the proposed six months of support valued at $1 million — chalkbeat.org/tennessee; search mgt memphis oversight board - nashville focal (october 23, 2026) — analysis of tennessee state education data on teacher retention: risen from the 2023-24 low, not back to earlier levels — focalnews.org; search tennessee teacher retention - tennessee firefly (october 22, 2026), reporting on an excelined report — 83,021 tennessee births in 2023 (about 4% fewer than 2007), public kindergarten enrollment down 5% in 2024, district gains in rutherford, montgomery, williamson, and wilson counties and losses in memphis-shelby county — tennesseefirefly.com; search excelined tennessee births enrollment - tennessee department of education — tennessee investment in student achievement (tisa) district accountability reports due november 1 — tn.gov/education

entries.t: [American Samoa] Education Daily — October 26, 2026: A Season Without a Budget
entries.x: School sports in American Samoa are running on a patchwork: the Athletics Office has closed, the Fiscal Year 2027 budget carries no money for sports events, a season kicked off on September 4 anyway, and an October 22 government release on special program…
entries.w: [american samoa] education daily — october 26, 2026: a season without a budget school sports in american samoa are running on a patchwork: the athletics office has closed, the fiscal year 2027 budget carries no money for sports events, a season kicked off on september 4 anyway, and an october 22 government release on special program budget reductions named sports again. alex and jordan walk the timeline from the august house education committee testimony to this week's reductions notice, and what families should ask their schools now. educational guidance, not legal advice. sources: - talanei / 93khj reporting via conven.org, 'no funding for school sports in fy2027 budget' — house education committee testimony (athletics office closed; sports under the secondary division and the american samoa high school athletics association; no fy2027 funding for sports events; business and ngo assistance not guaranteed; lawmaker response): https://conven.org/samoa/news/no-funding-for-school-sports-in-fy2027-budget/ - american samoa government, press releases index — pr001-09042026, 'the american samoa department of education proudly celebrates the official 2026 sports kick-off' (09/04/2026), and pr001-10222026, 'fy 2027 special program budget reductions to impact community services, sports, village development, and government activities' (10/22/2026): https://www.americansamoa.gov/pressreleases - american samoa department of education (asdoe) homepage — system totals (more than 12,000 students; 22 early childhood education sites, 23 elementary schools, 6 high schools; more than 1,900 employees), retrieved october 26, 2026: https://www.amsamoadoe.com to verify the press releases without a stable direct link: americansamoa.gov, then press releases, then the october 2026 and september 2026 listings by release number.

entries.t: [Iowa] Education Daily — October 26, 2026: Showing Up Again

entries.w: [iowa] education daily — october 26, 2026: showing up again iowa chronic absenteeism fell from 21.6 percent to 15.8 percent in one year, a record advanced placement year in des moines, and nearly one billion dollars in local bonds on the november third ballot. sources: - k-12 dive (october 2, 2026), progress to reduce chronic absenteeism slows nationwide — iowa 21.6 percent in 2023-24 to 15.8 percent in 2024-25, national 22.6 percent in 2025, 50 percent challenge averages 5.7 percent vs 3.2 percent: https://www.k12dive.com/news/progress-to-reduce-chronic-absenteeism-slows-nationwide/832029/ - the 74 (june 22, 2026), iowa declared war on chronic absenteeism. now it's gaining some ground — senate file 2435 thresholds at 10, 15 and 20 percent, three-year 9.8 point iowa decrease vs 5.9 nationwide, des moines 45.4 to 21.2 percent, davenport 42.5 to 33.2 percent, cedar rapids 38.6 to 27.8 percent, 80 des moines referrals: https://www.the74million.org/article/iowa-declared-war-on-chronic-absenteeism-now-its-gaining-some-ground/ - des moines public schools (october 22, 2026), dmps students reach record levels of ap participation and achievement — 3,993 students in ap as of october 1, 61 percent scored 3 or higher in spring 2026, up about 11 points in two years, 34 courses, five dollar reduced fee: https://www.dmschools.org/2026/10/dmps-students-reach-record-levels-of-ap-participation-and-achievement/ - itr local (october 21, 2026), nearly 1 billion dollars in local bonds on iowa's november ballot — search itrlocal.org for that title for the district-by-district table including hinton 8.6 million dollars, fairfield 24.85 million dollars and emmetsburg 25 million dollars; the live page may show a verification screen. - kirkwood communiqué via eagle voice, community to vote on 88 million dollar bond — search eaglevoice.com for that title for kirkwood community college's 88 million dollar november third referendum across 18 counties.

entries.t: [New Mexico] Education Daily — October 26, 2026: Showing Up Is Getting Better. Being Counted Still Isn't Fair.
entries.x: New Mexico's chronic absenteeism rate is falling — PED reports 38% in 2022-23 down to 28% in 2025-26 — yet an independent tracker still ranks the state highest in the nation, and students with disabilities and Native American students are absent at far higher…
entries.w: [new mexico] education daily — october 26, 2026: showing up is getting better. being counted still isn't fair. new mexico's chronic absenteeism rate is falling — ped reports 38% in 2022-23 down to 28% in 2025-26 — yet an independent tracker still ranks the state highest in the nation, and students with disabilities and native american students are absent at far higher rates, sometimes for therapies their own education plans require. sources: - new mexico public education department, fy28 budget proposal news release (sept. 24, 2026; chronic absenteeism 38% in 2022-23 to 28% in 2025-26): search ein presswire for 'ped proposes budget focused on student achievement, support' - futureed, tracking state trends in chronic absenteeism, updated oct. 20, 2026 (new mexico 31.25% in 2025-26, highest among 22 reporting states): https://www.future-ed.org/tracking-state-trends-in-chronic-absenteeism/ - legislative education study committee, bill analysis for sb105, attendance for success & excused absences (57th legislature, 2nd session, 2026): https://www.nmlegis.gov/sessions/26%20regular/lescanalysis/sb0105.pdf - senate bill 105 text (2026), amending the attendance for success act, section 22-12a nmsa 1978: https://www.nmlegis.gov/sessions/26%20regular/bills/senate/sb0105.html - public education department, bill analysis for sb105 (jan. 26, 2026; 2024-25 chronic absenteeism: students with disabilities 34.8%, native american students 37.3%, statewide 29.7%): https://www.nmlegis.gov/sessions/26%20regular/agencyanalysis/sb0105_924.pdf - las cruces public schools midyear strategic-plan board report (chronic absenteeism 24% at 80th-day count, down from ~33%): search citizen portal for 'district reports midyear gains on literacy and math; board hears updates on attendance and school supports'

entries.t: The Right That Stops at the Schoolhouse Door
entries.x: Lock the door, pull the shade, move the children to the hard corner. The lockdown drill is rehearsed in every school in America — and it is the closest thing public school teachers have to a workplace safety law. In this national episode, Alex and Jordan…
entries.w: the right that stops at the schoolhouse door lock the door, pull the shade, move the children to the hard corner. the lockdown drill is rehearsed in every school in america — and it is the closest thing public school teachers have to a workplace safety law. in this national episode, alex and jordan trace why: a single definition in the occupational safety and health act of 1970 wrote every public employee in the country out of the nation's workplace-safety law, and the right to a workplace free from recognized hazards stops at the schoolhouse door. we built the count from osha's own registry: in 29 of the 56 states, districts, and territories, a public school employee has a real safety regulator; in 27, there is no one to complain to. plus the bargain police and firefighters got and teachers never did, the idea collision that stops abatement where a student is the hazard, new york's 2024 law that proves the fix can be built, and new hampshire's paper right — a petition process aimed at a rulebook with no violence standard in it. the full written feature and the jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction coverage map are published with this story at educationacrossthestates.com. sources — osha, state plans (22 full plans covering private and public sector workers; 7 public-sector-only plans: connecticut, illinois, maine, massachusetts, new jersey, new york, u.s. virgin islands): https://www.osha.gov/stateplans ; occupational safety and health act of 1970, section 3(5) definition of "employer" and section 5(a)(1) general duty clause: https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/oshact/completeoshact and https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/oshact/section5-duties ; littler, "new york amends workplace violence prevention law to extend coverage to public schools" (labor law section 27-b, effective january 4, 2024): https://www.littler.com/news-analysis/asap/new-york-amends-workplace-violence-prevention-law-extend-coverage-public-schools ; parker & covert llp on california sb 553 / labor code section 6401.9 (written workplace violence prevention plans, including school districts, by july 1, 2024): https://www.parkercovert.com/new-requirements-for-california-employers-to-implement-workplace-violence-prevention-plans-by-july-2024 ; new hampshire rsa chapter 277 (277:13-a employee petition for inspection; 277:15-a post-incident inspections naming school districts): https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/xxiii/27

entries.t: [NH] Nashua School Board Watch — Correction: Finance & Operations Committee, October 19, 2026
entries.x: MINUTES CORRECTION: The formal minutes for the October 19, 2026 Finance & Operations Committee are now posted, and this watch checked them against our corrected report on that meeting, as promised. Most of the reporting is confirmed exactly — all seven…
entries.w: [nh] nashua school board watch — correction: finance & operations committee, october 19, 2026 minutes correction: the formal minutes for the october 19, 2026 finance & operations committee are now posted, and this watch checked them against our corrected report on that meeting, as promised. most of the reporting is confirmed exactly — all seven special education contract approvals passed 2-0 at the caps we reported (acm staffing $79,560, which also resolves the packet discrepancy we flagged; beyond words $46,800; champion speech therapy $90,935; slp mama-to-be amendment to $76,930; amergis $43,680; blazerworks $206,640; special education services $57,000 — $554,645 in new or expanded authority), the fy27 september transfer report was approved, and the solar power purchase agreements for main dunstable, birch hill, bicentennial, and the school administration building were approved. one money item was materially different: we reported three cerf vehicles totaling $223,523, including a $56,296 transit van; the minutes record approval of four purchases totaling $266,777.07 — dump truck $90,100, f-250 pickup $77,127, maverick pickup $34,407, and a field tractor $65,143.07, with no transit van. the minutes also record an information item we missed: a proposed joint city-school erp system at approximately $9 million (no vote taken). only two committee members were present, and every vote passed 2-0. also in this episode: the board of education did not meet on monday, october 26 as previously listed — the full board meets wednesday, october 28 at 5:00 pm to take up these recommendations (with the dump truck and maverick amounts already revised in that agenda), followed by the facilities master plan public hearing at 6:00 pm. official documents confirm a board meeting on november 16 but do not label it the facilities vote; that timing is unconfirmed. watch board meetings live via the meeting link on nashua.edu under the board of education section. listener poll: https://strawpoll.com/xvg718km6yr sources: - nashua school district, finance & operations committee minutes, october 19, 2026 (2-page pdf, linked from the finance and operations page on nashua.edu): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1b1fufvnta1nu-zfrund1ksdfvvezaof3/view?usp=drive_link - nashua school district, finance and operations agendas and minutes page (nashua.edu > our district > board of education > boe

entries.w: [washington] education daily — october 27, 2026: the seats that came back — on paper washington cut transition to kindergarten funding by twenty five percent this spring — now state officials have a phased plan to restore it, while thousands of new early learning slots show that awarded seats and open classrooms are not the same thing. sources: - ospi news release, april 9, 2026, 'school districts statewide face legislative cuts to critical early learning programs' (ospi.k12.wa.us, news center > news releases) — 157 districts, more than 7,000 tk students, 25 percent funding cut, nearly 2,000 fewer students, wakids readiness results across six domains. - citizen portal summary, october 14, 2026, 'ospi and dcyf outline ecap expansion and phased tk restoration plan to the legislature' — elac briefing: restore pre-cut tk funding first, then controlled growth; roughly 2,400 new eceap slots and 42 new sites, some awards returned for staffing, subcontracting, and facility constraints. - washington state pta and league of education voters summaries of essb 6260 and the 2026 supplemental budget — tk prioritization for existing programs and extreme child care deserts, eligibility criteria, and the funding reduction. - citizen portal summary, october 15, 2026, 'state board adopts 2027 legislative platform, urges full funding for basic education' — unanimous platform restoring tk funding; public comment on tk readiness. - ospi washington state learning standards review page (ospi.k12.wa.us, student success > learning standards > washington state learning standards review) and csta washington, 'survey for revised cs standards due dec 13' — computer science and educational technology survey open october 15 to december 13, 2026, announced in ospi bulletin b035-26 on october 14, 2026; standards last revised 2018, adoption scheduled second half of 2028.

entries.t: [Alaska] Deep Dive — Growing Its Own: Alaska's Permanent Educator Apprenticeship and the Special Education Vacancy It Has to Close
entries.x: How Alaska's permanently approved Educator Registered Apprenticeship turns paraprofessionals already working in classrooms into licensed special education teachers — the vacancy numbers it has to close, how the Anchorage and University of Alaska Fairbanks…
entries.w: [alaska] deep dive — growing its own: alaska's permanent educator apprenticeship and the special education vacancy it has to close how alaska's permanently approved educator registered apprenticeship turns paraprofessionals already working in classrooms into licensed special education teachers — the vacancy numbers it has to close, how the anchorage and university of alaska fairbanks models actually work, and the june 30, 2027 grant deadline that will decide whether it lasts. sources: alaska department of education and early development (deed), release dated july 15, 2026, 'alaska receives permanent federal approval for educator registered apprenticeship program' (content.govdelivery.com/accounts/akdeed/bulletins/420b89f — provisional approval december 3, 2024, permanent approval completed july 13, 2026, launch with 5 apprentices in january 2025, 96 apprentices for fall 2026, 13 districts, university and statewide partners); deed, educator registered apprenticeship program page (education.alaska.gov/t-rap — eligibility, teacher pathway up to 4 years with 5,000-6,000 on-the-job learning hours, principal pathway, available pathways including special education, state apprenticeship expansion fund 2 grant support through june 30, 2027); anchorage school district, teacher apprenticeship program page (asdk12.org — fall 2026 cohort of 5 special education and 10 elementary apprentices, tuition/books/praxis coverage, journey worker mentors, final-year co-teaching, four-year service commitment); university of alaska fairbanks school of education, teacher apprenticeship pathway (uaf.edu/soe/pathways/apprenticeship.php — two-year distance pathway, special education k-12 post-baccalaureate initial certificate and added endorsement routes); alaska beacon reporting by corinne smith, april 8, 2026, on the march 30, 2026 joint house and senate education committee testimony (alaskabeacon.com; also carried at alaskafirstmedia.com — 345 unfilled positions on the first day of school, nearly 200 special education vacancies, the vacancy tax, turnover costs and rates). to verify any item without a stable url, search education.alaska.gov for 'educator registered apprenticeship' and akleg.gov for the march 30, 2026 joint education committee hearing.

entries.w: [florida] education daily — october 28, 2026: florida's ai rule takes effect tomorrow tomorrow, october 29, 2026, florida's binding ai rule takes effect: amendments to rule 6a-1.0957 require parental opt-in before a student directly uses an ai instructional tool, a substantively comparable non-ai alternative for families who decline, a ban on companion and social-emotional ai, human review for grading, discipline, and exceptional student education referrals, and district policy amendments by july 1, 2027. sources: - rumbergerkirk, 'navigating the new ai rule: practical challenges and implementation guidance for florida school board employees' (updated october 16, 2026) — rule text analysis: effective october 29, 2026; july 1, 2027 adoption deadline; opt-in, prohibitions, agentic ai supervision and kill switch, human decision-maker rule, reporting and recordkeeping duties: https://www.rumberger.com/insights/navigating-the-new-ai-rule-practical-challenges-and-implementation-guidance-for-florida-school-board-employees/ - core learning exchange, 'florida made school ai opt-in. now earn the yes' (october 13, 2026) — unanimous state board adoption september 16, 2026; commissioner henry mack quote ('we are exercising the virtue of prudence here'); comparable-alternative analysis; college-level graded-work rule: https://www.corelearningexchange.com/blog/florida-ai-school-rules-2026.html - tc sentinel editorial, 'florida draws a line on ai in classrooms' (october 27, 2026) — the state's first-in-nation binding-standards claim, prek through college scope: https://www.tcsentinel.com/florida-draws-a-line-on-ai-in-classrooms-treasure-coast-schools-must-step-up-to-hold-it.html - rule text: florida administrative code rule 6a-1.0957, internet safety policy, as amended — search flrules.org for '6a-1.0957' for the adopted rule and its adoption history.

entries.w: [minnesota] deep dive — the commission that said no: minnesota's $250 million special education cut the blue ribbon commission was ordered to cut $250 million per biennium from minnesota special education aid while maintaining fape — and unanimously told the legislature not to do it. this deep dive walks through the charge, the enrollment and cross-subsidy numbers, each of the four savings recommendations in dollars (adsis, fin 728 transportation, charter tuition aid, and hold harmless), the automatic default cut that follows if the legislature does nothing, saint paul's $9 million-a-year exposure and its separate english learner vote due by october 30, fridley's updated audit scrutiny, and the permanent school fund amendment on the november 3 ballot where a blank counts as a no. sources: -
